Sparse Attention

Skipping work you can prove you don't need — and why most of it never reaches the wall clock.

§How to use this document

Part of a series with the Recurrent Depth & Looped Transformers, Linear Attention and LLM Inference Systems guides. This one is written with a hardware reader in mind: the recurring question is not "does this reduce FLOPs" but "does this reduce cycles, and what does the datapath have to look like for it to."

  • Pass 1. §0–§2. The cost structure of attention and why sparsity exists at all. Without this the rest is a list of acronyms.
  • Pass 2. §3–§6. The three eras, in order. The plot is: fixed patterns → the FlashAttention reset that invalidated most of them → inference-time patching → sparsity built into pre-training.
  • Pass 3. §7–§9. The hardware chapter, the evaluation traps, and a decision table.

Assumed background: attention as softmax⁡ ⁣(QK⊤d)V\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt d}\right)Vsoftmax(d​QK⊤​)V, what a KV cache is, and a rough sense of GPU memory hierarchy (registers / SRAM / HBM).

If a term is unfamiliar, it is defined. Appendix B explains the GPU vocabulary (SM, warp, CTA, tile, coalescing, TMA, systolic array) and the theory terms (Turing completeness, expander graphs, Pareto frontier, Ω notation) from scratch. Appendix C is a one-line glossary of the domain terms.

The thesis, up front

Attention is sparse in the math and dense in the memory system. Almost every failure in this literature comes from optimising the first and forgetting the second. The methods that shipped — NSA, MoBA, DSA — are the ones whose sparsity pattern is expressible as whole blocks that a tensor-core kernel can skip without a gather.

0Why sparse attention — and why most of it fails

Two different bottlenecks wear the same name.

0.1 Two regimes, two bottlenecks

Attention costs something completely different in the two phases of inference, and a method that helps one may do nothing for the other.

The mistake that invalidates half the papers

In decode, an "80% sparse" method that still reads the whole KV cache to decide what to skip has saved you nothing. Decode is bandwidth-bound; the arithmetic you skipped was free. Only sparsity that prevents bytes from crossing HBM counts. This is exactly SpAtten's criticism of the earlier A³ and MNNFast accelerators: they must fetch everything from DRAM before computing what can be pruned, so the DRAM traffic — the actual cost — is unchanged.

Derivation: derive the causal attention FLOPs and the GQA byte count

Assumptions and units. There are n prompt tokens, Hq query heads, Hkv KV heads, head width d, and b bytes per cached scalar. One multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. Count QKᵀ and AV only; projections, softmax, masks, index selection, and launch costs are additional. Set G=Hq/Hkv, assuming an integer number of query heads per KV group.

  1. A length-d dot product costs approximately 2d FLOPs. Multiplying its attention weight into a length-d value and accumulating also costs approximately 2d. Thus one query–key pair costs approximately 4d.
  2. Causal prefill has 1+2+…+n=n(n+1)/2 legal pairs per head. Multiply the pair count by 4dHq.
  3. At decode there is one new query per head and n cached positions, giving n pairs per head. Keys and values require two n×d arrays for each KV head. If a kernel reuses a loaded KV group across its G query heads, those bytes are loaded once per group.
Fprefill≈2Hqdn(n+1)≈2Hqdn2 FLOPsFdecode≈4Hqdn FLOPsMdecode≈2Hkvdnb bytesIdecode=FdecodeMdecode≈2Gb FLOP/byte\begin{aligned}F_{\mathrm{prefill}}&\approx2H_qdn(n+1)\approx2H_qdn^2\ \mathrm{FLOPs}\\ F_{\mathrm{decode}}&\approx4H_qdn\ \mathrm{FLOPs}\\ M_{\mathrm{decode}}&\approx2H_{\mathrm{kv}}dnb\ \mathrm{bytes}\\ I_{\mathrm{decode}}&=\frac{F_{\mathrm{decode}}}{M_{\mathrm{decode}}}\approx\frac{2G}{b}\ \mathrm{FLOP/byte}\end{aligned}Fprefill​Fdecode​Mdecode​Idecode​​≈2Hq​dn(n+1)≈2Hq​dn2 FLOPs≈4Hq​dn FLOPs≈2Hkv​dnb bytes=Mdecode​Fdecode​​≈b2G​ FLOP/byte​

For BF16, b=2, so one unshared query head has intensity approximately 1 FLOP/byte, and a perfectly reused G=8 group has approximately 8 FLOP/byte. Sparsifying n to k reduces both numerator and denominator by k/n; the intensity stays the same. Head sharing raises intensity, while skipping KV lowers traffic. These are different benefits. Repeated loads, metadata, and cache writes lower the achieved ratio; on-chip reuse must be measured rather than inferred from the model definition.

Exercise — Compute a decode step before choosing a sparse kernel

For n=65,536, d=128, Hq=32, Hkv=8 and BF16 KV, compute attention FLOPs, KV-read bytes, and ideal arithmetic intensity for one layer and one sequence. Repeat if selection keeps 4,096 positions with no extra overhead. Give MiB using 2²⁰ bytes.

Show worked solution

The theoretical attention traffic improvement is 16×, but not the whole-model speedup. Indexing, selected-page gathers, MLPs, and other layers remain; the next derivation accounts for them.

0.2 How much of the cost is attention anyway?

Worth calibrating, because the answer swings by orders of magnitude with context length.

  • Short context. Attention is a small minority of FLOPs; the MLPs dominate. Sparsifying attention is nearly pointless — this is why sparse attention was an academic topic from 2019–2022 and an industrial one from 2024.
  • Long context. DeepSeek's estimate: softmax attention accounts for 70–80% of total latency when decoding 64k-length contexts. At that point attention is the model.
  • The FLOPs/latency divergence. SpAtten's profiling of GPT-2 is the number to remember: attention takes over 50% of latency while being only ~10% of FLOPs, and ~73% of that time goes to data movement — splitting heads, K/V concatenation, reshape, transpose. Attention is a memory-system problem wearing a matmul costume.

0.3 The FLOP illusion

NSA's framing of why the field stalled is the clearest statement of the problem, and it is worth adopting as your own filter. Two failure modes:

  1. Phase-restricted sparsity. A method that sparsifies prefill but not decode (or vice versa) is amortised away by whichever phase it didn't touch. Methods designed around attention-score statistics from prefill often can't be applied at decode, where the query is a single token.
  2. Training-incompatible sparsity. Most methods apply sparsity at inference to a backbone pre-trained with full attention. The backbone never learned to live with the pattern, so accuracy degrades — and you also never get the training-side speedup, which for long-context models is where most of the cost actually is.

Add a third, purely mechanical one: a sparse pattern that a GPU cannot express as skipped tiles doesn't save time. A 90%-sparse mask with randomly scattered nonzeros runs slower than dense attention, because you pay gather overhead, lose coalescing, and still issue full tensor-core tiles for whatever fraction of each tile is live.

Derivation: turn an attention-kernel speedup into an end-to-end prediction

Model. Let the dense request latency be T. A measured fraction f is spent in the attention component that will be accelerated. The sparse kernel accelerates that component by s, and its additional selection/scheduling cost is hT. All other work is unchanged; this assumes no overlap change and no quality-driven increase in output length.

  1. The unchanged work costs (1−f)T.
  2. The accelerated attention costs fT/s.
  3. Add the new cost hT, then divide the baseline T by the result.
Tsparse=T[(1−f)+fs+h]Send-to-end=1(1−f)+f/s+hA win requiresh<f(1−1s)s→∞:S≤11−f+h\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{sparse}}&=T\left[(1-f)+\frac fs+h\right]\\ S_{\mathrm{end\text{-}to\text{-}end}}&=\frac1{(1-f)+f/s+h}\\ \text{A win requires}\quad h&<f\left(1-\frac1s\right)\\ s\to\infty:\quad S&\le\frac1{1-f+h}\end{aligned}Tsparse​Send-to-end​A win requireshs→∞:S​=T[(1−f)+sf​+h]=(1−f)+f/s+h1​<f(1−s1​)≤1−f+h1​​

For f=0.70, s=8, and h=0.05, the denominator is 0.30+0.0875+0.05=0.4375, so the request improves by approximately 2.29×. An 8× attention result is compatible with only a 2.29× request improvement. With f=0.10 and the same costs, the improvement is only 1/0.9625≈1.04×. This explains why context length and phase matter without declaring a universal context threshold. For a request with both prefill and decode, first sum their measured times and apply each phase’s own improvement.

Exercise — Diagnose a prefill-only speed claim

A request takes 120 ms in prefill and 880 ms in decode. A method makes prefill attention infinitely fast; attention is 80% of prefill. Decode is unchanged, and index construction adds 10 ms. What is the maximum request speedup?

Show worked solution

Only 0.8·120=96 ms can disappear. The new time is (120−96)+880+10=914 ms. The maximum improvement is 1000/914≈1.094×. The unchanged 880 ms decode phase dominates. The result is a ceiling under the stated decomposition, not a prediction that any real kernel reaches it.

1What can you actually skip?

"Sparse attention" conflates three different optimisations with three different beneficiaries. Separate them before reading any paper.

1.1 Three different savings

You save…By…Helps
ComputationNot computing qi⋅kjq_{i}\cdot k_{j}qi​⋅kj​ or the corresponding AVAVAV productPrefill. Nearly useless in decode.
Memory trafficNot loading those kkk, vvv vectors from HBMDecode, directly. This is the one that matters most.
Memory capacityPermanently discarding KV entries (eviction)Batch size / max context. Irreversible.
Selection vs. eviction — a distinction people blur

Selection keeps the full KV cache and chooses a read set per query; eviction permanently removes entries from the available cache unless another tier or recomputation can recover them. Selection can make a serious mistake for the current query, but it preserves the option of selecting a missed token later. Eviction reduces capacity demand as well as possible traffic, at the cost of stronger future-query risk. Neither policy is automatically safe; its error depends on omitted mass, value content, and downstream computation.

1.2 The four design axes

The Sparse Frontier taxonomy, which I find the most useful organising scheme in the literature:

AxisChoicesHardware consequence
Unit of sparsificationIndividual token · block of 64/128 contiguous tokens · KV page · head · layerDecides everything. Only block/page granularity maps to tensor-core tiles and coalesced loads.
Importance estimationContent-agnostic (fixed pattern: sinks + local window) · content-aware (top-k on estimated scores)Content-aware costs an extra scoring pass — which must itself be cheap enough not to eat the savings.
Budget allocationUniform across heads/layers · adaptive per head · fixed token budget · budget scaling with sequence lengthAdaptive budgets create load imbalance across warps/PEs. Uniform budgets waste effort on easy heads.
Cache managementKeep everything (selection) · evict (compression)Eviction shrinks the page table and raises achievable batch size; selection does not.

A fifth axis, implicit in the others but decisive in practice: when is the sparsity decided? Offline per head (MInference), online per query (Quest, DSA), learned during pre-training (NSA, MoBA), or learned as a separate small predictor (SeerAttention).

2Why sparsity exists in the first place

Sparse attention only works because trained attention maps really are sparse. It is worth seeing why, because the structure of the sparsity dictates the structure of the kernel.

2.1 Attention sinks

The mechanism is worth internalising because it recurs everywhere. Softmax must sum to one. When a query has no strong match anywhere in the context, it still has to put its probability mass somewhere — so models learn to dump it on a few tokens that every query can see. In a causal model the earliest tokens are visible to everyone, so they become the default sink, regardless of their semantic content. Four initial tokens suffice; with them, models trained with a 4K window handle 4 million tokens of streaming text stably, at up to 22.2× the speed of the recomputation baseline.

Design implication

Any eviction policy must special-case the first few tokens. Any positional scheme must too. And a follow-up result that is easy to miss: models deliberately pre-trained with a dedicated sink token don't need the heuristic at all — the sink is an artefact of the objective, not a law of nature.

2.2 Attention maps have shapes, and the shapes differ per head

Attention weights in long-context LLMs show up to 96.8% sparsity, but the sparsity is not uniform: it is head-specific and, for two of the three types, content-dependent. This is the empirical fact underneath every method in §5 and §6:

  • The positions of vertical and slash lines shift with the content, so a static mask cannot capture them — you need online index construction.
  • But the type of a head is stable, so it can be identified offline, once, per head.
  • And the non-zeros cluster spatially, so a block approximation loses little. This is the single most important fact for hardware: the natural sparsity of attention is approximately block-structured, which is exactly the structure a GPU can exploit.

Related and useful: heads specialise into retrieval heads, which genuinely need the whole context, and streaming heads, which only ever need sinks plus a local window. DuoAttention learns this split and gives a full KV cache only to the retrieval heads — a large capacity win at little accuracy cost.

Derivation: bound the error caused by dropping attention mass

One fixed attention row. Let aj=exp(sj)/Z be its dense normalized probabilities, and keep a set S. Let ε=Σj∉Saj, with ε<1. Assume the retained logits and values themselves are unchanged. Sparse softmax renormalizes the kept probabilities: ãj=aj/(1−ε) for j∈S.

  1. Define μS=Σj∈Sajvj/(1−ε) and, if ε>0, μD=Σj∉Sajvj/ε.
  2. The dense output is a mixture: o=(1−ε)μS+εμD. The sparse output is õ=μS.
  3. Subtract the outputs exactly, then apply the triangle inequality.
o−o~=ε(μD−μS)∥vj∥≤V ∀j  ⟹  ∥o−o~∥≤2εVmax⁡i,j∥vi−vj∥≤D  ⟹  ∥o−o~∥≤εD\begin{aligned}o-\widetilde o&=\varepsilon(\mu_D-\mu_S)\\ \|v_j\|\le V\ \forall j&\implies\|o-\widetilde o\|\le2\varepsilon V\\ \max_{i,j}\|v_i-v_j\|\le D&\implies\|o-\widetilde o\|\le\varepsilon D\end{aligned}o−o∥vj​∥≤V ∀ji,jmax​∥vi​−vj​∥≤D​=ε(μD​−μS​)⟹∥o−o∥≤2εV⟹∥o−o∥≤εD​

The diameter bound follows because both μ values are convex combinations: their difference is a weighted sum of pairwise value differences. No dropped entries means ε=0 and exact equality. At ε=0.01 and V=5, the bound is 0.1 in the chosen norm. It may be loose: discarded and retained values can be nearly identical. Conversely, low probability does not imply negligible effect if the values have large norm.

Limits. This is a local attention-output bound, not an end-to-end language-model quality guarantee. Later nonlinear layers can amplify perturbations, and dropping a sink changes the normalization of every remaining token. It does not prove why sinks emerge in training, that four sinks suffice for all checkpoints, or that historical attention scores predict future ε. Selection preserves the underlying cache and permits recovery on future queries; eviction removes that option.

Exercise — Find the exact error, then compare two bounds

A row has weights (0.5,0.3,0.2) and scalar values (2,4,−1). Drop the last entry. Compute the dense and sparse outputs, their error, the 2εV bound, and the diameter bound.

Show worked solution

The dense output is 0.5·2+0.3·4+0.2·(−1)=2.0. Retained mass is 0.8, so the sparse output is (1+1.2)/0.8=2.75. The absolute error is 0.75. Here ε=0.2, V=4 gives 2εV=1.6; the value diameter is 4−(−1)=5, giving εD=1.0. The exact mixture identity gives 0.2·|−1−2.75|=0.75. Both bounds hold, and the diameter bound is tighter.

3Era 1: fixed patterns (2019–2021)

Problems defining this stage. The initial problem was quadratic attention cost on long sequences. Fixed sparse graphs try to retain local processing and paths for long-range information without estimating relevance at runtime; their central limitation is that connectivity does not guarantee retrieval of the content a particular query needs.

Hand-designed masks with provable properties. Conceptually clean; almost none of them made it into production models. Understanding why is the point of this section.

The lineage, briefly:

  • Sparse Transformer

    Core idea. Use strided and fixed sparse patterns, together with block-sparse kernels, to replace dense interactions with structured subsets.

    (Child et al., 2019) — factorised attention into strided and fixed patterns, motivated by looking at the attention maps of a 128-layer model on CIFAR-10 and finding them already sparse. It also shipped block-sparse GPU kernels, which mattered more than the patterns.
  • Longformer

    Core idea. Combine sliding-window attention, optional dilation and designated global tokens to connect long documents through a sparse graph.

    (2020) — sliding window + dilation + task-specific global tokens. The practical workhorse of the era.
  • BigBird

    Core idea. Add random links to local windows and global tokens so a sparse graph supports wider information propagation; the theoretical constructions depend on their resource assumptions.

    (2020) — window + global + random, with theory: sparse transformers of this form are universal approximators of sequence functions (they can approximate any continuous sequence-to-sequence map to arbitrary accuracy, given enough width and depth) and are Turing complete (able to simulate any computation, given unbounded resources). Read the fine print — the constructions need a number of layers or global tokens that grows, so the theory says "not fundamentally weaker," not "free." See Appendix B for both terms.
Why this era didn't stick
  1. Content-agnostic masks lose retrieval. A fixed window cannot attend to the one relevant sentence 90K tokens back. Perplexity barely notices; needle-style tasks collapse.
  2. They require pre-training from scratch with the pattern — and the frontier models were all being trained dense.
  3. FlashAttention moved the goalposts (§4). A 2× theoretical FLOP reduction is not interesting against an exact baseline that just got 7× faster in wall clock.

What survived is the vocabulary — sink, window, global, dilation, block — and the sliding-window layer itself, which is alive and well as the cheap half of modern hybrid stacks (Gemma 3, GPT-OSS, Samba, and friends interleave small windows with occasional global layers).

Derivation: derive fixed-pattern receptive fields without overclaiming expressivity

Causal local window. Suppose each layer lets token t read positions t−w+1 through t, with no dilation and no additional global edges. A representation after ℓ layers depends on at most positions t−ℓ(w−1) through t. This is an induction: one layer extends the previous layer’s reachable interval by at most w−1 positions.

Reachable interval after ℓ layers:[max⁡(1,t−ℓ(w−1)),t]Distance D requires:ℓ≥⌈Dw−1⌉\begin{aligned}\text{Reachable interval after }\ell\text{ layers}:\quad&[\max(1,t-\ell(w-1)),t]\\ \text{Distance }D\text{ requires}:\quad&\ell\ge\left\lceil\frac D{w-1}\right\rceil\end{aligned}Reachable interval after ℓ layers:Distance D requires:​[max(1,t−ℓ(w−1)),t]ℓ≥⌈w−1D​⌉​

With w=256 and D=65,536, at least ceil(65,536/255)=258 layers are needed along this local graph. Adding a global node can reduce graph distance: if it can first read a source and a later query can read the updated global representation, information takes two attention layers. In a causal decoder, an initial token cannot aggregate future tokens; a global position must respect time ordering. Thus encoder global-token diagrams cannot be copied into a causal decoder unchanged.

Dilated or random edges can shorten paths, but short graph distance is a statement about possible information flow, not learned retrieval accuracy. A path may bottleneck many facts through a small state, and attention weights may not route the right fact. BigBird’s expressivity constructions carry their own depth, width, precision, and global-token assumptions. A mask’s diameter alone does not establish those theorems or guarantee quality at fixed model size.

4The FlashAttention reset

Problems defining this stage. The comparison changed when exact attention stopped materializing its quadratic score matrix in HBM. The problem became reducing actual memory transfers and execution time against an IO-efficient dense kernel, so the organization of retained work mattered as much as its amount.

Core idea. FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles using online softmax and recomputes intermediates in backward instead of writing the full score matrix to HBM. Its improvement comes from reducing IO rather than omitting attention pairs.

The most important paper in sparse attention is not a sparse attention paper. It is the one that proved the bottleneck was never FLOPs.

Two ideas, both of which you should be able to reconstruct from memory:

  1. Tiling with online softmax. Softmax looks non-decomposable because it needs a global max and a global sum. It isn't: keep a running max mmm and running sum ℓ\ell ℓ, and rescale the accumulator when a new tile raises the max (derivation in §A.2). This turns attention into a streaming reduction that never stores N×NN\times NN×N.
  2. Recomputation instead of storage. In the backward pass, recompute the attention tile on-chip from the stored m,ℓm, \ell m,ℓ rather than reading it from HBM. More FLOPs, less time — the clearest possible demonstration of the thesis.
IOstandard=Ω(Nd+N2)HBM accessesIOFlashAttention=O ⁣(N2d2M),M=SRAM sizeOften much smaller for realistic d,M.Matching lower bounds use the paper’ s computation modeland SRAM assumptions; not an unconditional hardware optimum.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{IO}_{\mathrm{standard}}&=\Omega(Nd+N^2)\quad\text{HBM accesses}\\ \mathrm{IO}_{\mathrm{FlashAttention}}&=O\!\left(\frac{N^2d^2}{M}\right),\quad M=\text{SRAM size}\\ &\text{Often much smaller for realistic }d,M.\\ &\text{Matching lower bounds use the paper' s computation model}\\ &\text{and SRAM assumptions; not an unconditional hardware optimum.}\end{aligned}IOstandard​IOFlashAttention​​=Ω(Nd+N2)HBM accesses=O(MN2d2​),M=SRAM sizeOften much smaller for realistic d,M.Matching lower bounds use the paper’ s computation modeland SRAM assumptions; not an unconditional hardware optimum.​
Consequences for everything after 2022
  • The dense baseline is now exact, memory-linear in sequence length, and very fast. Any approximate method must beat that, not the naive baseline.
  • The paper's own block-sparse variant is 2–4× faster than FlashAttention with IO complexity improving proportionally to the sparsity ratio — the template every later method follows.
  • Kernel granularity became a central design constraint. Skipping blocks or pages makes dense-tile execution and coalesced loading easier. Token-level selection can also save work when retained rows are gathered into a smaller tiled problem or handled by a suitable sparse kernel. NSA and MoBA emphasize block structure; DSA uses shared selected token indices. Nominal sparsity must be translated into actual instructions and memory transactions.

Successors worth knowing: FlashAttention-2 (better work partitioning, fewer non-matmul FLOPs, ~2× again), FlashAttention-3 (Hopper: warp-specialisation, TMA, FP8, asynchrony), and FlashDecoding, which splits the KV dimension across SMs because at batch-1 decode there is otherwise not enough parallelism to fill the GPU.

Derivation: reconstruct tiled softmax as an associative reduction

Setup. For one query, each tile T contains logits sj and values vj. Store a triple (mT,ℓT,uT) where mT=maxj∈Tsj, ℓT=Σexp(sj−mT), and uT=Σexp(sj−mT)vj. The output is u/ℓ, not u alone.

  1. For disjoint tiles A and B, choose a common maximum m=max(mA,mB).
  2. Rewrite each exponential as exp(s−m)=exp(s−mA)exp(mA−m), or the analogous B expression.
  3. Sum the rescaled denominators and weighted numerators.
ℓ=emA−mℓA+emB−mℓBu=emA−muA+emB−muBo=uℓ\begin{aligned}\ell&=e^{m_A-m}\ell_A+e^{m_B-m}\ell_B\\ u&=e^{m_A-m}u_A+e^{m_B-m}u_B\\ o&=\frac u\ell\end{aligned}ℓuo​=emA​−mℓA​+emB​−mℓB​=emA​−muA​+emB​−muB​=ℓu​​

This merge reproduces the same total exponential sums regardless of tile grouping, so it is associative in exact arithmetic. That enables streaming FlashAttention and split-KV/FlashDecoding reductions. The new common maximum prevents exponent overflow. Floating-point rounding still depends on merge order; “exact attention” means no deliberate model approximation, not bitwise equality across every kernel.

A singleton with s=2,v=3 has (m,ℓ,u)=(2,1,3); another with s=1,v=7 has (1,1,7). Merging gives ℓ=1+e⁻¹, u=3+7e⁻¹, and o≈4.0758. The algorithm needs scalar normalization state and a value-sized accumulator, not an n-sized probability row in HBM. It still computes every allowed score; tiling and sparsity change different parts of the cost.

Exercise — Merge tiles whose maxima differ substantially

Tile A has (m,ℓ,u)=(100,2,6), and B has (99,3,12), with scalar u. Compute the merged output without evaluating exp(100). Why is (6+12)/(2+3) wrong?

Show worked solution

The common maximum is 100. Scale B by e⁻¹: ℓ=2+3e⁻¹≈3.103638, u=6+12e⁻¹≈10.414553, so o≈3.355595. The naive ratio 18/5=3.6 combines sums normalized to different maxima and therefore changes their relative mass. Online softmax stores enough information to put both tiles onto a common exponential scale.

5Era 2: inference-time sparsity (2023–2024)

Problems defining this stage. These methods seek savings from already-trained dense models without retraining them. They must estimate which history matters cheaply enough to justify the estimate, while separating irreversible KV eviction from temporary read selection and prefill computation from decode traffic.

Take a dense pre-trained model and make its attention sparse at serving time. No retraining — which is the whole appeal and also the whole problem.

5.1 The methods, by what they target

MethodTargetsMechanismNote
StreamingLLM

Core idea. Retain attention-sink tokens and a rolling recent window, bounding decode-cache size while discarding the older non-sink history.

KV cache (decode)Fixed: 4 sinks + rolling windowContent-agnostic, so information outside the window is simply gone. Perfect for streaming, wrong for retrieval.
H2O

Core idea. Accumulate historical attention importance and keep heavy-hitter tokens alongside recent context, evicting lower-scoring KV entries.

KV cache (decode)Evict by accumulated attention score ("heavy hitters")Eviction based on historical scores; degrades notably when also applied to prefill.
SnapKV

Core idea. Use queries near the end of the prompt as an observation window to select a compact set of prompt KV entries for subsequent decoding.

KV cache (after prefill)Use the last window of queries to vote on which KV to keepThe "recent queries predict future importance" heuristic, used widely since.
Quest

Core idea. Store coordinate-wise key extrema per page and use the current query to rank pages with inexpensive score bounds before fetching selected KV pages.

Attention reads (decode)Query-aware top-k over KV pages, using per-page min/max key boundsSelection, not eviction. Page granularity — composes with PagedAttention.
MInference

Core idea. Identify each head’s characteristic sparse pattern, construct its indices online and dispatch a matching sparse prefill kernel.

Attention compute (prefill)Classify each head offline into A-shape / vertical-slash / block-sparse, build indices online, run pattern-specific kernelsPrefill only, but with real kernels and real speedups.
SparQ

Core idea. Estimate relevance using selected high-magnitude query channels, then fetch the chosen key/value rows at full width.

Attention reads (decode)Approximate scores using only the highest-magnitude channels of qqq, then fetch the top rows in fullA two-pass fetch: cheap approximate pass, exact narrow pass.
DuoAttention

Core idea. Separate retrieval heads from streaming heads, preserving broad history only where the learned head allocation needs it.

KV cache (capacity)Learn a per-head mask splitting retrieval heads from streaming headsHead granularity: the coarsest unit, and therefore the friendliest to implement.

5.2 What a careful evaluation found

Core idea. The Sparse Frontier evaluates training-free sparsity across methods, model families, tasks and budgets under controlled comparisons. Its contribution is to expose where nominal savings survive quality constraints and where aggregate scores hide task-specific failures.

The Sparse Frontier (Nawrot et al., 2025) is the largest controlled study of training-free sparse attention — six methods, multiple model families and sizes, sequences to 128K, sparsity to 0.95, nine tasks. Its conclusions are the practical state of the art and several are uncomfortable:

  1. Sparse attention is genuinely worth it at the Pareto level. A larger sparse model beats a smaller dense one at matched cost. That is the honest way to state the benefit — not "80% fewer FLOPs."
  2. Fine-grained per-query importance estimation during prefill is impractical today — both because estimating it costs too much and because no kernel converts that fine granularity into wall-clock time. You are forced into a task-dependent choice between global-to-token and block-to-block selection.
  3. Decode is friendlier. At decode, token-to-page selection is feasible and generalises better, tolerating higher sparsity.
  4. Longer sequences tolerate more sparsity — so a fixed token budget, which is what most production deployments use, is systematically the wrong shape. Budgets should scale with sequence length.
  5. There is no universally safe sparsity level. Aggregate metrics hide large per-task degradations; some tasks fall off a cliff at moderate sparsity while others are fine at 0.95.
The structural limitation of the whole era

These methods impose a sparsity pattern on a model that was pre-trained to expect every token. The model has no opportunity to route information differently, to learn which tokens it will need later, or to compensate. That is the gap Era 3 closes — and it is why the production long-context models of 2025–2026 all trained their sparsity in.

Derivation: derive Quest’s page bound and its selection limits

Page metadata. For every key coordinate c in page P, store lc=minj∈Pkjc and uc=maxj∈Pkjc. For a query q, choose u when qc≥0 and l when qc<0, because multiplication by a negative number reverses an inequality.

∀j∈P:q⊤kj=∑cqckjc≤∑c:qc≥0qcuc+∑c:qc<0qclc=UPScaled dot product bound=UPd\begin{aligned}\forall j\in P:\quad q^\top k_j&=\sum_c q_c k_{jc}\\ &\le\sum_{c:q_c\ge0}q_cu_c+\sum_{c:q_c<0}q_cl_c=U_P\\ \text{Scaled dot product bound}&=\frac{U_P}{\sqrt d}\end{aligned}∀j∈P:q⊤kj​Scaled dot product bound​=c∑​qc​kjc​≤c:qc​≥0∑​qc​uc​+c:qc​<0∑​qc​lc​=UP​=d​UP​​​

Example: q=(2,−1), l=(−1,0), u=(3,4). Every key in the page has qᵀk≤2·3−0=6. The coordinate extrema may belong to different keys, so no key need actually attain 6. Quest uses this inexpensive page score to choose which pages deserve full-resolution attention. The min/max inequality is rigorous; selecting a fixed number of pages by those bounds is still an approximation unless an additional threshold certificate proves that every omitted page is irrelevant. High upper bounds can be loose.

Traffic check. With n positions, page size P, key width d, bm bytes per metadata scalar, bv bytes per KV scalar, and k retained positions, one group reads roughly 2⌈n/P⌉dbm+2kdbv2\lceil n/P\rceil d b_m+2kdb_v2⌈n/P⌉dbm​+2kdbv​ bytes, ignoring indices. Divide by dense 2ndbv2ndb_v2ndbv​ to get an approximate ratio bmPbv+kn\frac{b_m}{Pb_v}+\frac knPbv​bm​​+nk​. For P=64, equal scalar sizes and k/n=1/16, the ratio is 1/64+1/16=5/64≈7.81%, an ideal 12.8× traffic reduction rather than 16×. This assumes cached metadata and contiguous page loads; building the metadata, gathering, and short final pages add cost. Quest primary paper.

Exercise — An upper bound is not a page-ranking oracle

Page A contains keys (10,0) and (0,10); page B contains (6,6) twice. For q=(1,1), compute each min/max upper bound and true maximum dot product. Which page would a top-one bound selector choose, and where is the true maximum?

Show worked solution

A’s coordinate maxima are (10,10), so UA=20, but both actual scores are 10. B has UB=12 and true maximum 12. A top-one bound selector chooses A and misses B, which contains the highest actual score. The coordinatewise bound is valid for each page; ranking by bounds does not preserve ranking by actual maxima. This is a counterexample to exact selection, not to the inequality.

6Era 3: native, trainable sparsity (2025–2026)

Problems defining this stage. Training can teach the model to route information through the limited paths that inference will retain. The central task becomes jointly designing a cheap relevance signal, a useful retained representation, and an execution pattern that turns the learned sparsity into lower cost.

A chronological progression from NSA and MoBA to DSA, then DeepSeek-V4 and V4.1: learned selection, sequence compression and cross-layer memory sharing. Hardware-friendly sharing can use blocks or a common token set; not every method requires block-granular selection.

6.1 NSA — hierarchy plus a hardware-aligned kernel

Core idea. NSA combines compressed global context, selected fine-grained blocks and a local window. Its branches preserve complementary information while shared selection and block execution make the retained attention easier to reuse across query heads.

Two design decisions are the whole paper:

  1. Derive the selection scores from the compression branch. The expensive part of content-aware sparsity is scoring. NSA gets its scores as a by-product of an attention computation it was doing anyway, so the selection overhead is close to free.
  2. Make the kernel GQA-aware. The kernel loads queries by GQA group in a grid loop, then fetches the corresponding sparse KV blocks in an inner loop, computing on SRAM. Because all heads in a group share the same selected blocks, one KV block load is amortised across the whole group — which is what keeps arithmetic intensity high enough to stay on the tensor cores (§7.3).

NSA has since been picked up by NVIDIA's cuDNN frontend as an experimental module with Blackwell-optimised kernels — selection, compression and top-k in CUTLASS/CuTe, sliding window through the cuDNN backend. That is about as strong a signal as exists that a sparsity pattern is hardware-realisable.

6.2 MoBA — mixture-of-experts, applied to context

Core idea. MoBA scores context blocks using their pooled keys and routes each query to a small subset of blocks. It then computes ordinary attention over the selected tokens, transferring the conditional-computation idea of MoE from experts to context.

MoBA⁡(q,K,V)=Softmax⁡(qK[I]⊤)V[I]I=⋃i:gi>0Ii(selected blocks)gi=1{si∈TopK⁡({sj},k)}si=⟨q,mean_pool⁡(K[Ii])⟩\begin{aligned}\operatorname{MoBA}(q,K,V)&=\operatorname{Softmax}(qK[I]^\top)V[I]\\ I&=\bigcup_{i:g_i>0}I_i\quad\text{(selected blocks)}\\ g_i&=\mathbf1\{s_i\in\operatorname{TopK}(\{s_j\},k)\}\\ s_i&=\langle q,\operatorname{mean\_pool}(K[I_i])\rangle\end{aligned}MoBA(q,K,V)Igi​si​​=Softmax(qK[I]⊤)V[I]=i:gi​>0⋃​Ii​(selected blocks)=1{si​∈TopK({sj​},k)}=⟨q,mean_pool(K[Ii​])⟩​

The design philosophy is explicitly "less structure": don't impose a window or a sink, let the router discover the pattern. Sliding-window attention and attention sinks both fall out as special cases of fixed gating, which makes MoBA a strict generalisation of Era 1. It also transitions smoothly between sparse and full attention, which is what lets it be added to an existing model by continued pre-training. It serves Kimi's long-context traffic in production.

The honest caveat, stated in the paper: MoBA needs continued training. It is not a drop-in for a frozen checkpoint.

Derivation: relate block-centroid routing to the actual attention mass

Notation. In one block of P keys, let μ=P⁻¹Σkj and δj=kj−μ. For fixed q define c=qᵀμ/√d and ej=qᵀδj/√d. The exact unnormalized probability mass of this block is Σexp(c+ej). Factoring out the shared centroid term gives:

log⁡Zblock=c+log⁡P+log⁡ ⁣(1P∑jeej)1P∑jej=0  ⟹  log⁡ ⁣(1P∑jeej)≥0(Jensen)∣ej∣≤Δ ∀j  ⟹  0≤log⁡ ⁣(1P∑jeej)≤Δ\begin{aligned}\log Z_{\mathrm{block}}&=c+\log P+\log\!\left(\frac1P\sum_j e^{e_j}\right)\\ \frac1P\sum_je_j=0&\implies\log\!\left(\frac1P\sum_je^{e_j}\right)\ge0\quad\text{(Jensen)}\\ |e_j|\le\Delta\ \forall j&\implies0\le\log\!\left(\frac1P\sum_je^{e_j}\right)\le\Delta\end{aligned}logZblock​P1​j∑​ej​=0∣ej​∣≤Δ ∀j​=c+logP+log(P1​j∑​eej​)⟹log(P1​j∑​eej​)≥0(Jensen)⟹0≤log(P1​j∑​eej​)≤Δ​

MoBA’s centroid score c therefore omits a dispersion correction. Equal-sized blocks with similar within-block score dispersion can be ranked well by c; a block with one unusually relevant key can have large true mass despite a modest mean. For unequal block sizes, even the log P term matters. This is why routing by a pooled key is a learned approximation to token attention, not an algebraic identity. Training can make representations easier to route, but the derivation does not prove it will.

NSA’s compressed branch has a related distinction: attention over learned summary tokens does not generally equal the sum of dense attention weights in the original block. Its compression scores are useful routing signals because the architecture is trained jointly. The compression, selected-token, and local-window outputs are combined by learned gates; unless those gates are normalized and branches partition probability mass appropriately, the result should be understood as a learned mixture of operators, not a decomposition of one exact softmax row.

Exercise — Quantify a centroid-routing failure

Ignore the √d scale. Block A has token scores (3,−3), and block B has scores (1,1). Both blocks contain two tokens. Which block has the larger centroid score? Which has the larger true unnormalized mass?

Show worked solution

Centroids are cA=0 and cB=1, so mean-score routing prefers B. Exact masses are ZA=e³+e⁻³≈20.1353 and ZB=2e≈5.4366, so A has approximately 3.70× more mass. A’s positive dispersion correction is log(cosh 3)≈2.3093; B’s is zero. The example isolates information lost by averaging keys.

6.3 DSA — a cheap indexer in front of expensive attention

Core idea. DSA uses a comparatively cheap learned indexer to rank history positions before the more expensive main attention reads them. Training aligns this routing signal with attention importance, so selection is part of the learned computation rather than a post-training eviction heuristic.

It,s=∑jwt,jIReLU⁡(qt,jI⋅ksI)St={s:It,s∈Top-k⁡(It,:)},k=2048\begin{aligned}I_{t,s}&=\sum_jw^I_{t,j}\operatorname{ReLU}(q^I_{t,j}\cdot k^I_s)\\ S_t&=\{s:I_{t,s}\in\operatorname{Top\text{-}k}(I_{t,:})\},\quad k=2048\end{aligned}It,s​St​​=j∑​wt,jI​ReLU(qt,jI​⋅ksI​)={s:It,s​∈Top-k(It,:​)},k=2048​

Why the indexer is cheap: few heads, small embedding dimension, FP8, and an MQA-style design in which all heads share one set of selected KV tokens. It is still O(N2)O(N^{2})O(N2) in principle — the win is entirely in the constant factor, and in the fact that the expensive MLA attention afterwards is O(N⋅k)O(N\cdot k)O(N⋅k).

The training recipe is the transferable part:

  1. Dense warm-up. Freeze everything except the indexer, keep attention dense, and train the indexer to imitate the real attention distribution: sum the main attention scores across heads, L1-normalise along the sequence, and minimise DKL(p∥softmax⁡(I))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\operatorname{softmax}(I))DKL​(p∥softmax(I)). 1000 steps, ~2.1B tokens.
  2. Sparse training. Switch on top-k selection and train everything, still aligning the indexer but now only over the selected set. 15000 steps, ~944B tokens. The indexer's input is detached from the main graph so the two objectives don't fight.
What the three have in common
  1. Trained, not retrofitted. All three either pre-train with the pattern or do substantial continued training.
  2. Cheap scoring, expensive attention. All three separate a low-precision, low-dimension scoring pass from the full-precision attention pass. The scorer is the architectural innovation; the attention is ordinary.
  3. Coarse units. Blocks (NSA, MoBA) or a shared per-query token set with head sharing (DSA). Nobody ships per-head unstructured top-k.
  4. Kernels shipped with the paper. Every one of them includes a custom kernel. A sparsity pattern without a kernel is a research artefact.

A note on the ecosystem cost, which is easy to underestimate: vLLM reported that DSA's indexer complicates continuous batching and paged attention, and required quantising the MLA latent and indexer keys written into the page table. Sparse attention is not a local change to a kernel — it reaches into the memory manager.

Derivation: derive the indexer’s KL gradient and a conditional coverage guarantee

Detached teacher. Let p be a normalized teacher importance distribution over eligible positions and q=softmax(I) be the indexer’s distribution. Treat p as fixed when differentiating the auxiliary indexer loss, as in DSA’s detached training path. The teacher may aggregate heads; it is then a proxy for importance rather than each head’s exact attention row.

  1. Write DKL(p∥q)=Σpjlog pj−ΣpjIj+logΣexp I.
  2. The first term is constant with respect to I. The derivative of log-sum-exp with respect to Ij is qj.
  3. Therefore ∂D/∂Ij=qj−pj: training raises underestimated positions and lowers overestimated ones.
∣p(S)−q(S)∣≤TV⁡(p,q)TV⁡(p,q)≤DKL(p∥q)2(natural logarithms)p(Sc)≤q(Sc)+DKL(p∥q)2\begin{aligned}|p(S)-q(S)|&\le\operatorname{TV}(p,q)\\ \operatorname{TV}(p,q)&\le\sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)}2}\quad\text{(natural logarithms)}\\ p(S^c)&\le q(S^c)+\sqrt{\frac{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)}2}\end{aligned}∣p(S)−q(S)∣TV(p,q)p(Sc)​≤TV(p,q)≤2DKL​(p∥q)​​(natural logarithms)≤q(Sc)+2DKL​(p∥q)​​​

If top-k selection retains 98% of q’s mass and the measured full-distribution KL is 0.0008, the bound permits at most 0.02+√0.0004=0.04 omitted teacher mass. Combine with the earlier value-norm bound only if p is the same attention row whose output is being approximated. An aggregated teacher, selected-set-only training loss, or an unmeasured full-distribution KL does not satisfy that premise. In particular, a loss computed only after selection cannot by itself certify important mass outside the selected set.

The indexer still touches many candidate positions. If its per-position cost is a fraction c of the full attention cost and the expensive attention keeps fraction r, a first-order cost ratio is c+r plus top-k/kernel overhead. With c=0.03 and r=0.02, the arithmetic ceiling is 20×, before overhead; replacing r by zero cannot exceed 1/c≈33.3×. Fixed k does not make the full algorithm independent of n while the indexer scans n entries.

Exercise — What does a small selected-set KL fail to prove?

An indexer assigns probabilities (0.495,0.495,0.005,0.005), while the teacher assigns (0.01,0.01,0.49,0.49). The selected set is the first two positions. Compute the KL between distributions renormalized onto that set and the teacher mass omitted. Explain why a perfect selected-set loss can coexist with poor routing.

Show worked solution

Renormalization onto the selected set gives (0.5,0.5) for both distributions, so the selected-set KL is exactly zero. But the teacher mass outside the set is 0.49+0.49=0.98. The loss has removed the very quantity needed to evaluate routing coverage. A full-distribution objective or another mechanism that explores/corrects omitted positions is required to address that failure; zero conditional KL is not zero global KL.

6.4 DeepSeek-V4: compress the history before selecting it

Core idea. V4 first compresses historical representations, then combines access to compressed global history with a local window. CSA selects among compressed entries with an indexer, whereas HCA attends over a more aggressively compressed history directly.

April 2026 preview → June 2026 technical report. The next step after DSA is to reduce how many global entries exist, while retaining a short uncompressed local path.

Chronology and scope. DSA in V3.2 selects from a token-indexed history. V4 combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) with Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA). September’s V4.1-Flash then replaces this hybrid with CSA2 and cross-layer reuse. These are trained model architectures: replacing attention in an arbitrary checkpoint does not reproduce their accuracy. See the official release chronology, V4 report, and V4.1 report.

The compressor changes the object being retrieved

CSA uses learned, channel-wise weighted pooling over two adjacent blocks, emitting one entry per mmm tokens. The overlap spans 2m2m2m source positions; it does not change the output rate to one per 2m2m2m. A lightweight indexer scores these summaries, and MQA attends directly to selected summaries plus recent uncompressed entries. HCA instead pools nonoverlapping larger blocks and attends to every resulting summary. V4 §2.3.

aj,r=exp⁡(zj,r+bj,r)∑u∈Biexp⁡(zu,r+bu,r)cˉi,r=∑j∈Biaj,rcj,rCSA:∣Bi∣=2m,stride=m,M≈N/mHCA:∣Bi∣=m′,stride=m′,M′≈N/m′St=TopK⁡(index⁡(qt,kˉ1,…,kˉM))CSA reads={cˉi:i∈St}∪local_window⁡(t)HCA reads={cˉ1,…,cˉM′}∪local_window⁡(t)\begin{aligned}a_{j,r}&=\frac{\exp(z_{j,r}+b_{j,r})}{\sum_{u\in B_i}\exp(z_{u,r}+b_{u,r})}\\ \bar c_{i,r}&=\sum_{j\in B_i}a_{j,r}c_{j,r}\\ \mathrm{CSA}:\quad |B_i|&=2m,\quad\mathrm{stride}=m,\quad M\approx N/m\\ \mathrm{HCA}:\quad |B_i|&=m\prime,\quad\mathrm{stride}=m\prime,\quad M\prime\approx N/m\prime\\ S_t&=\operatorname{TopK}(\operatorname{index}(q_t,\bar k_1,\ldots,\bar k_M))\\ \mathrm{CSA\ reads}&=\{\bar c_i:i\in S_t\}\cup\operatorname{local\_window}(t)\\ \mathrm{HCA\ reads}&=\{\bar c_1,\ldots,\bar c_{M\prime}\}\cup\operatorname{local\_window}(t)\end{aligned}aj,r​cˉi,r​CSA:∣Bi​∣HCA:∣Bi​∣St​CSA readsHCA reads​=∑u∈Bi​​exp(zu,r​+bu,r​)exp(zj,r​+bj,r​)​=j∈Bi​∑​aj,r​cj,r​=2m,stride=m,M≈N/m=m′,stride=m′,M′≈N/m′=TopK(index(qt​,kˉ1​,…,kˉM​))={cˉi​:i∈St​}∪local_window(t)={cˉ1​,…,cˉM′​}∪local_window(t)​

Why this is not ordinary downsampling. Each channel has its own pooling weights. For two tokens and two channels, the compressor can favor token A’s first channel and token B’s second channel. The resulting vector need not equal either original token. It is a learned representation, not a losslessly encoded list. Consequently, an attention score against a summary is not generally the sum of attention scores against its constituent tokens.

Derivation — why compression changes attention

Take one-dimensional keys k1=−a,k2=ak_{1}=-a, k_{2}=ak1​=−a,k2​=a and equal pooling, giving summary kˉ=0\bar k=0kˉ=0. For query q, the original block contributes exp⁡(−qa)+exp⁡(qa)=2cosh⁡(qa)\exp(-qa)+\exp(qa)=2 \operatorname{cosh}(qa)exp(−qa)+exp(qa)=2cosh(qa) to the softmax denominator. A single pooled key contributes exp⁡(qkˉ)=1\exp(q\bar k)=1exp(qkˉ)=1. Even correcting for block length by multiplying by 2 leaves a factor cosh⁡(qa)\operatorname{cosh}(qa)cosh(qa). That factor depends on q and cannot be recovered from the mean alone. Learned compression must therefore be trained to preserve task-relevant information; it is not an exact algebraic factorization of dense attention.

Derive the storage, arithmetic and causality consequences

Let N be context length, H query heads, d the shared KV width, dᵢ the indexer key width, Hᵢ its query-head count, k the selected-entry count, w the local window, and p/pᵢ bytes per stored main/indexer element. Ignore constant-size unfinished compression state and metadata initially. A shared key/value latent is counted once; inserting the conventional factor of two would overcount this representation.

One CSA layer:Bglobal≈Nm(dp+dipi)Blocal≈wdplocalFindex/query≈2HidiNmFcore/query≈4Hd[min⁡(k,N/m)+w]One HCA layer:Bglobal≈Nm′dpFcore/query≈4Hd(N/m′+w)FCSA,prefill index≈∑t=1N2Hiditm≈HidiN2m\begin{aligned}\text{One CSA layer:}\quad B_{\mathrm{global}}&\approx\frac Nm(dp+d_ip_i)\\ B_{\mathrm{local}}&\approx wdp_{\mathrm{local}}\\ F_{\mathrm{index/query}}&\approx2H_id_i\frac Nm\\ F_{\mathrm{core/query}}&\approx4Hd[\min(k,N/m)+w]\\ \text{One HCA layer:}\quad B_{\mathrm{global}}&\approx\frac N{m\prime}dp\\ F_{\mathrm{core/query}}&\approx4Hd(N/m\prime+w)\\ F_{\mathrm{CSA,prefill\ index}}&\approx\sum_{t=1}^N2H_id_i\frac tm\approx\frac{H_id_iN^2}{m}\end{aligned}One CSA layer:Bglobal​Blocal​Findex/query​Fcore/query​One HCA layer:Bglobal​Fcore/query​FCSA,prefill index​​≈mN​(dp+di​pi​)≈wdplocal​≈2Hi​di​mN​≈4Hd[min(k,N/m)+w]≈m′N​dp≈4Hd(N/m′+w)≈t=1∑N​2Hi​di​mt​≈mHi​di​N2​​

The factor 4 in main attention counts both QK and AV with two operations per multiply-add. Softmax, projections, pooling, top-k, partial positional transforms and memory-layout overhead are excluded. The important conclusion is specific: a fixed k bounds core attention, while the indexer still grows with N; HCA retains a linear decode term and a quadratic prefill term with a much smaller coefficient. None of these equations alone predicts wall-clock throughput.

Causal readiness. A compressed entry may be exposed only once all source tokens it contains are available. Otherwise a training query could read a summary containing future tokens. Completed blocks are globally readable; the unfinished tail remains in state, and local attention handles recent fine-grained dependencies. This also explains why a prefix-cache implementation needs both immutable compressed pages and mutable local/compressor state.

Worked context. At N=1,048,576, CSA m=4 produces 262,144 global entries, while HCA m′=128 produces 8,192. Flash’s CSA main attention accesses at most 512+128=640 entries per query, whereas its indexer still examines the 262,144-entry compressed history. The indexer can therefore become the next optimization target even though the main sparse kernel is already fast.

Reported result and its scope

The official model card reports V4-Pro at 1M context using 27% of V3.2’s single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of its KV cache. This is a comparison between complete model configurations; it is not an isolated CSA ablation or a universal 3.7× latency speedup. Model dimensions, the layer mix and kernel implementation matter.

6.5 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: share the history across layers

Core idea. V4.1 shares compressed history across layers and separates full indexing, reindexing and selection reuse. This attacks repeated cache storage and repeated routing work as distinct costs, with hierarchical search further restricting later candidate scans.

September 2026. Once attention reads fewer entries, duplicated cache ownership and repeated indexing become increasingly expensive.

CSA2 removes the CSA/HCA mixture. Its three layer modes separate creating global memory, choosing memory and reading memory. The compressor drops overlap and its absolute positional bias; indexer keys are projected from main KV. Each layer retains its own attention query and local SWA state. V4.1 §2.3.

ModeMain KV + indexer KSelected addressesWhat is saved?
FullCreated hereComputed hereBaseline within CSA2
ReindexShared from FullRecomputed with own indexer QGlobal storage / generation
ReuseShared from FullShared from Full/ReindexGlobal storage and indexing

Let f(l) identify the Full layer whose cache layer l reads, and r(l) identify the layer supplying its selected set. A useful abstraction is:

Cℓ=Cf(ℓ),Kℓindex=Kf(ℓ)indexSℓ={TopK⁡(score⁡(qℓindex,Kf(ℓ)index)),Full / ReindexSr(ℓ),Reuseoℓ=Attention⁡(qℓ,Cf(ℓ)[Sℓ]∪SWAℓ)Bstored=∑f∈unique Full ownersbytes⁡(Cf,Kfindex)+∑ℓbytes⁡(SWAℓ)+Bstate/metadata\begin{aligned}C_\ell&=C_{f(\ell)},\quad K^{\mathrm{index}}_\ell=K^{\mathrm{index}}_{f(\ell)}\\ S_\ell&=\begin{cases}\operatorname{TopK}(\operatorname{score}(q^{\mathrm{index}}_\ell,K^{\mathrm{index}}_{f(\ell)})),&\text{Full / Reindex}\\ S_{r(\ell)},&\text{Reuse}\end{cases}\\ o_\ell&=\operatorname{Attention}(q_\ell,C_{f(\ell)}[S_\ell]\cup\mathrm{SWA}_\ell)\\ B_{\mathrm{stored}}&=\sum_{f\in\text{unique Full owners}}\operatorname{bytes}(C_f,K_f^{\mathrm{index}})\\ &\quad+\sum_\ell\operatorname{bytes}(\mathrm{SWA}_\ell)+B_{\mathrm{state/metadata}}\end{aligned}Cℓ​Sℓ​oℓ​Bstored​​=Cf(ℓ)​,Kℓindex​=Kf(ℓ)index​={TopK(score(qℓindex​,Kf(ℓ)index​)),Sr(ℓ)​,​Full / ReindexReuse​=Attention(qℓ​,Cf(ℓ)​[Sℓ​]∪SWAℓ​)=f∈unique Full owners∑​bytes(Cf​,Kfindex​)+ℓ∑​bytes(SWAℓ​)+Bstate/metadata​​

This equation shows why merely caching indices cannot deliver the same memory saving: it removes repeated top-k work, but every layer can still own an independent C. Conversely, sharing C does not remove scoring unless S is also shared. Reindex supplies an intermediate choice: preserve layer-specific retrieval while keeping common memory.

Hierarchical indexing: bound later searches, retain one full search

The decoder’s first Full layer scores the history, selects its own 512 entries, and constructs a larger pool using block-maximum scores. Up to 2,048 blocks of eight entries yield 16,384 candidates; four later Reindex layers choose within that pool. The restriction is introduced during post-training. Official V4.1 model card.

Derivation — the correct asymptotic claim

Suppose J indexers independently scan M positions and each score costs c. Baseline cost is cJM. With one initial scan and a shared pool of P positions, cost becomes c[M+(J−1)min⁡(M,P)]c[M+(J-1)\min(M,P)]c[M+(J−1)min(M,P)], plus block/top-k work. Thus:

Sindex≈JMM+(J−1)min⁡(M,P)M=1,048,576,P=16,384,J=5Sindex≈5,242,8801,114,112≈4.71lim⁡M→∞Sindex=J(J,P fixed)\begin{aligned}S_{\mathrm{index}}&\approx\frac{JM}{M+(J-1)\min(M,P)}\\ M&=1{,}048{,}576,\quad P=16{,}384,\quad J=5\\ S_{\mathrm{index}}&\approx\frac{5{,}242{,}880}{1{,}114{,}112}\approx4.71\\ \lim_{M\to\infty}S_{\mathrm{index}}&=J\quad(J,P\text{ fixed})\end{aligned}Sindex​MSindex​M→∞lim​Sindex​​≈M+(J−1)min(M,P)JM​=1,048,576,P=16,384,J=5≈1,114,1125,242,880​≈4.71=J(J,P fixed)​

This is an analytical comparison of decoder scoring, not a measured end-to-end speedup. The first scan survives. Encoder indexers and all non-indexer operations survive too. “Constant cost” applies to the later bounded searches, not the complete model.

Reproduce 890 bytes per token, including scales

The released schedule has three encoder Full owners at compression ratio 2, and one decoder Full owner at ratio 1. Main KV uses 512 E2M1 values plus one E4M3 scale per 16 values; indexer K uses 128 MXFP4 values plus one scale byte per 32. Main KV omits the tensor-level scale of full NVFP4. Local SWA remains FP8. Precision specification; layer schedule.

B(d,b,g,s)=db+⌈d/g⌉s8 bytesbeffective=b+sg(g∣d)Bmain=512⋅48+5121688=288 bytesBindex=128⋅48+1283288=68 bytesBentry=288+68=356 bytesBglobal(N)=356[3⌊N2⌋+N]Bglobal(N)N⟶356(32+1)=890 bytes/token\begin{aligned}B(d,b,g,s)&=\frac{db+\lceil d/g\rceil s}{8}\ \mathrm{bytes}\\ b_{\mathrm{effective}}&=b+\frac sg\quad(g\mid d)\\ B_{\mathrm{main}}&=\frac{512\cdot4}{8}+\frac{512}{16}\frac88=288\ \mathrm{bytes}\\ B_{\mathrm{index}}&=\frac{128\cdot4}{8}+\frac{128}{32}\frac88=68\ \mathrm{bytes}\\ B_{\mathrm{entry}}&=288+68=356\ \mathrm{bytes}\\ B_{\mathrm{global}}(N)&=356\left[3\left\lfloor\frac N2\right\rfloor+N\right]\\ \frac{B_{\mathrm{global}}(N)}N&\longrightarrow356\left(\frac32+1\right)=890\ \mathrm{bytes/token}\end{aligned}B(d,b,g,s)beffective​Bmain​Bindex​Bentry​Bglobal​(N)NBglobal​(N)​​=8db+⌈d/g⌉s​ bytes=b+gs​(g∣d)=8512⋅4​+16512​88​=288 bytes=8128⋅4​+32128​88​=68 bytes=288+68=356 bytes=356[3⌊2N​⌋+N]⟶356(23​+1)=890 bytes/token​

Why the accounting works. Each of the three encoder owners emits half as many entries as input tokens; the decoder owner emits one per token. Reuse/Reindex layers do not allocate another copy. At 1,000,000 tokens, this is 890 MB in decimal units, about 849 MiB, before allocator padding, local windows, unfinished state, batch metadata and any device replication. Four-bit labels alone would incorrectly predict 800 bytes/token: the missing 90 bytes/token are scales.

Why the model architecture changes prefix-cache economics

In Causal Encoder–Decoder (CED), decoder global KV is projected from the last encoder hidden states. Most prompt tokens therefore need only encoder computation plus cache projections. Decoder local SWA still needs initialization. The deployment uses bounded replay of a recent window instead of exact reconstruction through the full local receptive field. Persistent global cache and short-lived SWA state have different retention policies. CED; inference system.

Derivation — why replaying one window is approximate

With a causal local window of w positions, one layer’s output can depend on w−1 earlier positions. After L layers, the furthest dependency may be L(w−1) positions back. Initializing an entire trailing window adds another boundary-width term depending on the state being reconstructed. Therefore exact reconstruction has an O(Lw) history horizon. Replaying only w tokens removes potentially valid paths through the earlier boundary.

Jreplay=[max⁡(s,t−w+1),t]Jfull=[t−w+1,t]The sets differ near s; higher layers propagate differences.\begin{aligned}\mathcal J_{\mathrm{replay}}&=[\max(s,t-w+1),t]\\ \mathcal J_{\mathrm{full}}&=[t-w+1,t]\\ &\text{The sets differ near }s;\text{ higher layers propagate differences.}\end{aligned}Jreplay​Jfull​​=[max(s,t−w+1),t]=[t−w+1,t]The sets differ near s; higher layers propagate differences.​

Small measured accuracy degradation is an empirical property of the trained model and workload; it is not equality of hidden states. Cache-hit position can affect reconstructed states. This distinction matters when testing reproducibility or combining replay with a claim of distribution-preserving speculative decoding.

Cfull≈aNLCCED≈aNL2+awL2+CprojectionCCEDCfull≈12+w2N(ignoring projection)N≫w  ⟹  CCEDCfull→12\begin{aligned}C_{\mathrm{full}}&\approx aNL\\ C_{\mathrm{CED}}&\approx aN\frac L2+aw\frac L2+C_{\mathrm{projection}}\\ \frac{C_{\mathrm{CED}}}{C_{\mathrm{full}}}&\approx\frac12+\frac w{2N}\quad\text{(ignoring projection)}\\ N\gg w&\implies\frac{C_{\mathrm{CED}}}{C_{\mathrm{full}}}\to\frac12\end{aligned}Cfull​CCED​Cfull​CCED​​N≫w​≈aNL≈aN2L​+aw2L​+Cprojection​≈21​+2Nw​(ignoring projection)⟹Cfull​CCED​​→21​​

The approximation assumes similar per-layer costs; routed experts, kernel efficiency and cache hits change the actual timing. A 2× reduction in modeled layer work does not guarantee 2× lower time to first token. The same accounting explains storage: if a previous persistent cache contains equal global and SWA bytes, quartering global storage and ceasing to persist SWA gives G/4G+G=18\frac{G/4}{G+G}=\frac18G+GG/4​=81​. That ratio depends on the old workload’s composition; it is not a universal multiplier for every session.

What improved, and what still needs measuring?

StagePrimary savingRemaining risk / cost
V3.2 DSASelect token-level history for main attentionHistory remains stored; lightweight global scan
V4 CSA/HCACompress sequence and combine selective/full-summary coverageCompression discards information; independent layer caches; CSA scans summaries
V4.1 CSA2Share global caches and selected addresses; quantize entriesShared representations constrain layers; quantization and candidate-pool omissions
CED + replayReduce prefill work and long-lived local-state storageApproximate reconstruction; suffix length and hit rate affect benefit

Research implication. Compare capacity, traffic and compute separately. Sharing a physical cache across layers saves capacity immediately; it saves HBM reads only if a serving kernel or on-chip cache actually reuses the fetched entries. Different per-layer queries still require different QK/AV work. Likewise, smaller stored values require dequantization, so the value of FP4 depends on which resource is limiting the attention kernel.

Evaluation protocol. Report long-range retrieval and multi-hop tasks alongside ordinary language benchmarks; isolate compressor, sharing, precision and replay ablations; measure prefix-hit and prefix-miss paths; sweep context, batch size and output length; separate peak cache capacity from bytes moved and time per token. The published whole-model results establish feasibility, but changes in training data, parameter count and post-training prevent attributing every accuracy gain to attention alone.

Exercise — can index reuse alone produce 890 bytes/token?

Keep the V4.1 entry formats, but allocate independent caches in all 18 encoder CSA2 layers at m=2 and all 20 decoder layers at m=1. Compute global bytes/token. Then determine the reduction achieved by the actual sharing schedule.

Show worked solution

The hypothetical independent layout needs 356(18/2+20)=10,324356(18/2+20)=10,324356(18/2+20)=10,324 bytes/token. Actual sharing needs 356(3/2+1)=890356(3/2+1)=890356(3/2+1)=890. The ratio is 10,324/890=11.610,324/890=11.610,324/890=11.6. This is a controlled layout comparison at fixed formats and layer counts, not the report’s comparison against V4-Flash. Sharing only the selected indices leaves the 10,324-byte global KV allocation intact.

Exercise — when does the hierarchical pool provide no scoring saving?

Use the index-work equation above. What happens when the available context M is smaller than the pool limit P? Why can the hierarchical implementation still be slower in that case?

Show worked solution

Then min⁡(M,P)=M\min(M,P)=Mmin(M,P)=M and both methods score JMJMJM positions. Block scoring, pool construction and dispatch may add overhead without reducing scoring work. A practical implementation should specialize or bypass the hierarchy for short contexts; asymptotic long-context gains do not prove a win at every length.

7Making sparsity real in hardware

The chapter that decides whether any of this ships. If you design silicon, this is the section to argue with.

7.1 The three hidden costs of a sparse kernel

Every sparse attention kernel pays three taxes that dense attention does not. A method is only a win if its savings exceed all three.

TaxWhat it isMitigation in practice
Index / scoringYou must decide what to skip, and the decision itself costs compute and often a pass over memory.Reuse work you already do (NSA's compression branch); use a low-precision, low-dim scorer (DSA's FP8 indexer); pool keys per block so scoring is O(n/B)O(n/B)O(n/B) (MoBA).
GatherThe surviving KV entries are scattered in memory. Gathering them breaks coalescing and may serialise HBM transactions.Select whole contiguous blocks or pages so each "gather" is one large sequential burst. This is the real reason block granularity dominates.
Load imbalanceDifferent queries/heads keep different numbers of blocks, so warps, CTAs or PEs finish at different times and the slowest sets the pace.Fixed top-kkk (same budget for every query) instead of thresholding; share the selected set across a GQA group or across heads.
The rule of thumb

Sparsity pays only when bytes not moved×cost per byte\text{bytes not moved}\times\text{cost per byte}bytes not moved×cost per byte exceeds index cost+gather inefficiency+imbalance idle time\text{index cost}+\text{gather inefficiency}+\text{imbalance idle time}index cost+gather inefficiency+imbalance idle time. On a modern GPU the crossover is usually somewhere around 4–8× theoretical sparsity at block granularity, and essentially never reached at element granularity.

7.2 The granularity ladder

From finest to coarsest, with the honest verdict on each:

GranularityExampleVerdict on a tensor-core machine
ElementMagnitude pruning of the attention matrixUseless. The matrix is never materialised; there is nothing to prune.
Token (single K/V row)H2O, token top-k selectionEviction can compact the cache; selection can gather retained rows into tiles. Efficiency depends on row layout, head sharing, the gather implementation, and how many memory transactions are avoided.
Block (64–128 tokens)NSA, MoBA, block-sparse FlashThe sweet spot. Matches the K/VK/VK/V tile a Flash-style kernel loads; one decision skips one whole tensor-core tile.
Page (16–256 tokens)Quest, paged selectionSame benefits, and it composes with PagedAttention's existing page table — often the cheapest thing to implement in a real serving stack.
HeadDuoAttention, SpAtten head pruningTrivial to implement, large capacity savings, coarse accuracy control. Underrated.
LayerCross-layer KV sharing, hybrid stacksThe coarsest and most effective lever of all — and the one that is really an architecture decision, not a kernel one.

Why 64–128 and not 8? Because the block must be at least as large as the KKK-tile a warp-level matmul consumes; below that you issue a tensor-core instruction and throw most of its output away. On Hopper/Blackwell with TMA, the block should also be large enough to amortise a descriptor-driven bulk copy. If you are designing an accelerator, the equivalent question is: how many KV rows does one systolic-array pass consume? That number is your minimum useful block.

Derivation: convert element sparsity into executed tiles and a break-even test

A deliberately simple occupancy model. Suppose each score is independently retained with probability r, and a kernel must execute an entire t×t tile if any entry is retained. A tile is skipped only when all t² entries are absent. Independence is not realistic for clustered attention; it is a diagnostic for why unstructured sparsity may disappoint.

Pr⁡(tile executed)=1−(1−r)t2r=0.01, t=16:1−0.99256≈0.9237\begin{aligned}\Pr(\text{tile executed})&=1-(1-r)^{t^2}\\ r=0.01,\ t=16:&\quad1-0.99^{256}\approx0.9237\end{aligned}Pr(tile executed)r=0.01, t=16:​=1−(1−r)t21−0.99256≈0.9237​

Thus 99% element sparsity can still execute approximately 92% of tiles. Correlated block sparsity instead lets r directly approximate the fraction of executed tiles. A token/page selection kernel may have different granularity and need not obey this toy score-tile model; sparse execution should be measured at the hardware’s actual unit of work.

Let dense KV traffic be M, retained traffic fraction be rb, effective dense bandwidth be B, sparse bandwidth efficiency relative to dense be η, and index/launch cost be ti. Assuming non-overlapped costs, Tsparse≈ti+rbMηBT_{\mathrm{sparse}}\approx t_i+\frac{r_bM}{\eta B}Tsparse​≈ti​+ηBrb​M​ versus Tdense≈MBT_{\mathrm{dense}}\approx\frac MBTdense​≈BM​. Divide both sides by M/B:

Sparse wins⟺tiM/B+rbη<1S≈1ti/(M/B)+rb/η\begin{aligned}\text{Sparse wins}\quad&\Longleftrightarrow\quad\frac{t_i}{M/B}+\frac{r_b}{\eta}<1\\ S&\approx\frac1{t_i/(M/B)+r_b/\eta}\end{aligned}Sparse winsS​⟺M/Bti​​+ηrb​​<1≈ti​/(M/B)+rb​/η1​​

For 10% retained traffic, η=0.5 and selection costing 15% of dense time, the predicted speedup is 1/(0.15+0.20)≈2.86×, not 10×. Load imbalance, different query budgets, and overlap require a richer model. No single sparsity percentage guarantees a speedup independently of layout and runtime.

Exercise — Decide whether sparsity helps before implementing it

Dense attention takes 2 ms. A candidate keeps 25% of its traffic but achieves only half the dense bandwidth; selection and launches cost 0.8 ms. Is it faster? What is the largest overhead that still permits a strict win?

Show worked solution

The sparse traffic costs 2·0.25/0.5=1 ms. Total sparse time is 1.8 ms, so speedup is 2/1.8≈1.111×. To win strictly, overhead must be less than 2−1=1 ms. At exactly 1 ms the methods tie. If gathering lowered bandwidth efficiency below 0.25/(1−0.8/2)=5/12≈0.4167, this candidate would stop winning.

7.3 Arithmetic-intensity balancing — NSA's real contribution

The subtlest idea in the modern literature, and the one most worth stealing.

One head:F≈2Bd⏟qk+2Bd⏟av=4BdM≈2Bd sizeof(keys and values)I≈2sizeof=1 FLOP/byte(BF16)Shared GQA set:F≈4GBdM≈2Bd sizeof(same KV reused)I≈2Gsizeof=G FLOP/byte(BF16)\begin{aligned}\text{One head:}\quad F&\approx\underbrace{2Bd}_{qk}+\underbrace{2Bd}_{av}=4Bd\\ M&\approx2Bd\,\mathrm{sizeof}\quad\text{(keys and values)}\\ I&\approx\frac2{\mathrm{sizeof}}=1\ \mathrm{FLOP/byte}\quad\text{(BF16)}\\ \text{Shared GQA set:}\quad F&\approx4GBd\\ M&\approx2Bd\,\mathrm{sizeof}\quad\text{(same KV reused)}\\ I&\approx\frac{2G}{\mathrm{sizeof}}=G\ \mathrm{FLOP/byte}\quad\text{(BF16)}\end{aligned}One head:FMIShared GQA set:FMI​≈qk2Bd​​+av2Bd​​=4Bd≈2Bdsizeof(keys and values)≈sizeof2​=1 FLOP/byte(BF16)≈4GBd≈2Bdsizeof(same KV reused)≈sizeof2G​=G FLOP/byte(BF16)​

This is why NSA's kernel loads by GQA group and why DSA makes all heads share one selected token set. Sparsity reduces the numerator and the denominator together, so naive sparse decode has the same terrible arithmetic intensity as dense decode — you go faster only in proportion to bytes saved. Sharing the selection across heads is what lets you also move up the roofline. A sparse-attention design that does not share its selection across heads is leaving the larger win on the table.

7.4 What the sparse-attention ASICs teach

Problems defining this stage. Architecture work asks where selection happens relative to expensive data movement. A useful design must account for score estimation, top-k selection and irregular execution, because pruning arithmetic after fetching all its operands may save little in memory-bound decoding.

There is a decade of architecture work here, and the interesting part is how much of it was invalidated by the software — and which parts weren't.

DesignMechanismWhat it got right / wrong
A³

Core idea. Approximate relevance from sorted extreme key components, then prune low-scoring candidates before the remaining attention arithmetic.


(HPCA 2020)		Pre-sort each dimension of the keys; approximate the score using only the largest/smallest components; threshold-prune.Elegant approximate scoring — but it must fetch all keys from DRAM before it can prune, so it optimises only compute-bound (encoder) workloads. Useless for generative decode.
SpAtten

Core idea. Use cumulative token/head importance for cascading pruning and progressively fetch precision, reducing later work and operand traffic.


(HPCA 2021)		Cascade token + head pruning, an O(n)O(n)O(n) top-kkk engine with zero-eliminators, and progressive quantization.The right target: 10× DRAM access reduction, because pruning happens before the fetch. Token pruning 3.8×, head pruning 1.1×, progressive quantization 5.1×. Also the first to take generative (memory-bound) models seriously.
Sanger

Core idea. Predict a sparse mask with a low-precision pass, then map the selected attention work onto a reconfigurable systolic array.


(MICRO 2021)		Predict the attention mask with a quantized low-precision pass, then run a reconfigurable systolic array over the resulting dynamic sparsity.The predict-then-compute structure is exactly what NSA and DSA do four years later in software. Its reconfigurable PE array addresses load imbalance directly — the problem GPUs still solve by brute force.
Energon

Core idea. Apply successive low-precision filters to narrow the relevant keys at runtime instead of committing immediately to one coarse pruning decision.


(2021)		Multi-round low-precision filtering to find important keys at runtime.Criticises SpAtten's permanent cascade pruning as too coarse without retraining — a fair point that Era 3 answers by training the sparsity in.
The transferable lessons
  1. Prune before you fetch. This is the single organising principle. A pruning decision that requires the data it prunes is worthless in a memory-bound regime.
  2. A top-kkk engine is real silicon. Every modern method ends in a top-kkk. On a GPU this is a sort or a partial reduction, and at block granularity with n/Bn/Bn/B candidates it is cheap. At token granularity with n=128Kn = 128Kn=128K it is not. SpAtten's dedicated O(n)O(n)O(n) top-kkk engine with zero-eliminators is the kind of unit a purpose-built inference chip should have.
  3. Progressive precision. SpAtten fetches low bits first, decides, and only fetches the rest if needed — 5.1× on its own. This maps directly onto the modern "cheap FP8 indexer, expensive BF16 attention" split, and a chip that supports mixed-precision fetch granularity gets it for free.
  4. What did not transfer: fine-grained unstructured masks. Every design that assumed you can efficiently skip individual score elements was overtaken by tiled dense kernels. Build for blocks.

7.5 A checklist for silicon

If you are specifying an inference accelerator and want it to run 2026-era sparse attention well:

  • Cheap low-precision scoring path. FP8/INT8 MACs with a narrow datapath, usable independently of the main tensor unit, so the indexer runs concurrently with attention on the previous block.
  • Hardware top-kkk. Over n/Bn/Bn/B block scores, streaming, with a fixed kkk. Fixed kkk is what keeps the downstream schedule static.
  • Block-descriptor DMA. A gather engine whose unit is a KV block, not a cache line — give it a list of block IDs and let it issue coalesced bursts. This is the single most valuable piece of hardware for sparse attention.
  • Sharing across heads in the datapath. One KV block load feeding GGG query heads (GQA group) or all heads (MQA indexer). This is the arithmetic-intensity lever from §7.3 and it has to be expressed in the datapath to be real.
  • Enough SRAM for one KV block × group. The working set is B×d×2×precisionB\times d\times2\times\mathrm{precision}B×d×2×precision. Size SRAM so that a block, once fetched, is never re-fetched.
  • Mixed-precision fetch. The ability to load the high bits of a KV entry, decide, and then optionally load the low bits.
  • Do not build: fine-grained sparsity support at element granularity, or anything that assumes a static mask. Modern patterns are dynamic and content-dependent; the mask changes every token.

8Evaluating without fooling yourself

Sparse attention is unusually easy to evaluate badly, and the literature is full of examples.

  1. Perplexity is nearly blind to sparsity. Most tokens are predictable from local context, so a sliding window keeps perplexity almost intact while destroying long-range retrieval. Never report perplexity alone.
  2. Needle-in-a-haystack is too easy. A single verbatim needle in irrelevant filler is recoverable by almost any method that keeps sinks and does approximate retrieval. Use RULER or multi-hop / aggregation-style tasks that require many spread-out positions at once.
  3. Compare at iso-cost, not iso-sparsity. "95% sparse" means nothing across methods with different scoring overheads. Plot accuracy against measured latency or measured bytes moved.
  4. Report the worst task, not the average. The aggregate hides cliffs; some tasks degrade sharply at sparsity levels where the mean looks flat.
  5. Sweep sequence length. Sparsity tolerance rises with length, so a method tuned at 32K may be unnecessarily conservative at 128K and a method validated at 128K may be unsafe at 8K.
  6. Measure prefill and decode separately. They are different problems (§0.1) and a combined number lets a prefill-only method claim a decode win.
  7. Include the index cost in the measurement. Surprisingly often it is excluded.

9Decision guide

Your situationWhat to use
Frozen checkpoint, need decode-time speed and memoryPage-granular selection (Quest-style) on top of PagedAttention, with sinks always retained. Selection over eviction unless capacity is the binding constraint.
Frozen checkpoint, prefill-dominated (long prompts, short answers)MInference-style offline per-head pattern classification with pattern-specific kernels. The one place training-free sparsity clearly works.
Frozen checkpoint, HBM capacity is the wallHead-level split (DuoAttention) plus KV quantization. Coarse, safe, large.
Streaming / unbounded context, no retrieval requirementStreamingLLM. It is four sinks and a rolling window; nothing else is this cheap.
You control pre-trainingNSA or MoBA. This is where the real wins are, in training as well as inference.
You control continued training of a large modelDSA-style indexer + top-k, or MoBA. Both were designed to be retrofitted by continued training rather than from scratch.
You are designing the chip§7.5. Optimise for block-descriptor DMA, a streaming top-kkk, and mixed-precision fetch. Assume the mask is dynamic.
Context is short (<8K)Do nothing. Attention is not your bottleneck; go optimise the MLPs and the KV layout.

10Open problems

  1. Sparsity that survives RL post-training. The V4 and V4.1 systems now include substantial post-training, but controlled attention-specific ablations across RL stages remain important. Long-CoT RL can change attention statistics substantially, and the DeepSeek-V3.2 report itself attributes some benchmark regressions to the model generating fewer reasoning tokens. The remaining question is which routing budgets and shared representations remain robust across changes in tasks, reasoning length and RL policy.
  2. Budgets that scale with length. The evidence says tolerance grows with sequence length, yet every deployed system uses a fixed kkk. Nobody has a principled schedule.
  3. Composition with everything else. Sparse attention has to coexist with paged KV, continuous batching, speculative decoding and quantized caches. Each pair interacts badly in a different way, and the integration cost is routinely larger than the kernel work.
  4. A real theory of what is safe to drop. We have heuristics (sinks, heavy hitters, retrieval heads) and no predictive account of which tokens a future query will need. The indexer-learning approach (DSA) is the current best answer and it is purely empirical.
  5. Hardware for dynamic gather. GPUs do coalesced bursts well and irregular gathers badly. The gap between "the pattern we want" and "the pattern the memory system likes" is where the remaining factor of 2–4× lives.
  6. Sparse + linear hybrids. Sparse attention bounds the read set; linear attention bounds the state. They attack the same cost from opposite directions and the combination is barely explored — see the companion linear-attention guide.
