  2. start hereYuan et al. — Native Sparse Attention (ACL 2025). arXiv:2502.11089. §2 ("Rethinking Sparse Attention Methods") is the best critique of the field; §3 is the design.
  3. Nawrot et al. — The Sparse Frontier: Sparse Attention Trade-offs in Transformer LLMs (2025). arXiv:2504.17768. The honest evaluation. Read before believing any speedup claim, including your own.
  4. Xiao, Tian, Chen, Han & Lewis — Efficient Streaming LMs with Attention Sinks (ICLR 2024). arXiv:2309.17453. The sink phenomenon; short and worth reading in full.
  5. Jiang et al. — MInference 1.0 (NeurIPS 2024). arXiv:2407.02490. Head-type taxonomy and prefill kernels.
  6. Lu et al. — MoBA: Mixture of Block Attention (2025). arXiv:2502.13189. Short, clear, and the FlashAttention integration section is a good kernel-design read. Code: MoonshotAI/MoBA.
  7. DeepSeek-AI — DeepSeek-V3.2 (2025). arXiv:2512.02556. §2 for DSA and the two-stage indexer training recipe; Fig. 3 for the cost curves. See also the V3.2-Exp report for the original DSA description.
  8. Wang, Zhang & Han — SpAtten (HPCA 2021). arXiv:2012.09852. The one architecture paper to read: cascade pruning, the top-kkk engine, progressive quantization, and an honest latency breakdown. Code: mit-han-lab/spatten.
  9. Ham et al. — A³ (HPCA 2020) and Lu et al. — Sanger (MICRO 2021). The approximate-scoring and predict-then-compute traditions; Sanger's reconfigurable array is the best answer anyone has given to sparse load imbalance.
  10. Tang et al. — Quest (ICML 2024). arXiv:2406.10774. Query-aware page selection; the cleanest decode-time selection method.
  11. Beltagy et al. — Longformer (arXiv:2004.05150) and Zaheer et al. — BigBird (arXiv:2007.14062). Era 1, for the vocabulary and the theory.
  12. Zhang et al. — H2O (arXiv:2306.14048) and Xiao et al. — DuoAttention (arXiv:2410.10819). Eviction and head-level splitting.

A.1 What sparsity is worth, in bytes

A.2 Online softmax, derived

The identity that makes tiled attention possible. Process the keys in tiles; after each tile keep the running max mmm and running sum ℓ\ell ℓ, and rescale.

m1=max⁡(x1)ℓ1=∑jex1j−m1,o1=∑jex1j−m1v1jm2=max⁡(m1,max⁡(x2))ℓ2=em1−m2⏟rescale old sumℓ1+∑jex2j−m2o2=em1−m2o1+∑jex2j−m2v2jofinal=oℓ\begin{aligned}m_1&=\max(x_1)\\ \ell_1&=\sum_j e^{x_{1j}-m_1},\quad o_1=\sum_je^{x_{1j}-m_1}v_{1j}\\ m_2&=\max(m_1,\max(x_2))\\ \ell_2&=\underbrace{e^{m_1-m_2}}_{\text{rescale old sum}}\ell_1+\sum_je^{x_{2j}-m_2}\\ o_2&=e^{m_1-m_2}o_1+\sum_je^{x_{2j}-m_2}v_{2j}\\ o_{\mathrm{final}}&=\frac o\ell\end{aligned}m1​ℓ1​m2​ℓ2​o2​ofinal​​=max(x1​)=j∑​ex1j​−m1​,o1​=j∑​ex1j​−m1​v1j​=max(m1​,max(x2​))=rescale old sumem1​−m2​​​ℓ1​+j∑​ex2j​−m2​=em1​−m2​o1​+j∑​ex2j​−m2​v2j​=ℓo​​

Two consequences. First, memory for the attention matrix is O(block2)O(\mathrm{block}^2)O(block2), not O(N2)O(N^{2})O(N2), so attention becomes linear in memory — which is why FlashAttention enabled long context at all. Second, storing just (m,ℓ)(m, \ell )(m,ℓ) per row lets the backward pass recompute the attention tile on-chip instead of reading it from HBM. Both properties survive when you skip blocks, which is why block-sparse attention drops straight into the same kernel: skipping a tile means simply not updating (m,ℓ,o)(m, \ell , o)(m,ℓ,o) for it.

BBackground concepts

The GPU vocabulary, the theory terms and the notation this guide assumes. Skip what you know.

B.1 GPU and accelerator vocabulary

Most of §4 and §7 is unreadable without these. They are given in the order the hardware nests them.

TermMeaning, and why it matters here
SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)The independent compute unit of an NVIDIA GPU — an H100 has 132. Each has its own register file, shared memory (SRAM) and schedulers. "Not enough parallelism to fill the GPU" always means "fewer independent work items than SMs."
Warp32 threads that execute in lockstep — the real unit of scheduling. If one thread in a warp does more work than the others, the rest idle. This is the mechanism behind "load imbalance" in §7.1.
CTA / thread blockCooperative Thread Array: a group of warps scheduled together on one SM, able to share its SRAM. A sparse-attention kernel typically assigns one CTA per query block.
Tensor coreA matrix multiply–accumulate unit for supported tile shapes and precisions. A dense instruction does not become cheaper because individual operands are zero. Useful sparse execution must omit instructions, compact operands, or use supported hardware sparsity, while accounting for indexing and data movement.
TileThe fixed-shape sub-block of a matrix that one tensor-core instruction or one kernel iteration processes. "Skipping a tile" is the only sparsity a tiled kernel can exploit.
CoalescingWhen the threads of a warp read consecutive addresses, the memory system merges them into one wide transaction. Scattered reads do not merge, so a gather can cost several times the transactions of a contiguous read for the same bytes. This is the "gather tax" of §7.1.
SRAM vs HBMOn-chip scratchpad (tens of MB, ~19 TB/s on H100) versus off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (tens of GB, ~3.35 TB/s). Roughly 6× the bandwidth and a fraction of the latency, but thousands of times smaller. Every IO-aware algorithm is an argument about what to keep in SRAM.
TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator)A Hopper-generation DMA engine that copies a whole multidimensional tile between HBM and SRAM from a single descriptor, asynchronously. It rewards large contiguous blocks and penalises small scattered ones — another force pushing sparsity toward coarse granularity.
CUTLASS / CuTeNVIDIA's open C++ template libraries for writing high-performance GEMM and attention kernels. "Implemented in CUTLASS" means someone wrote a real fused kernel, not a PyTorch composition — the difference between a paper and a product.
TritonA Python-embedded language for writing GPU kernels at tile granularity. Most research kernels in this literature (NSA, FlashLinearAttention) ship as Triton.
Systolic arrayThe alternative to SIMT used by TPUs and most ASICs: a rigid 2-D grid of multiply–accumulate cells through which data flows rhythmically. Extremely efficient for dense matmul of the right shape, and very unforgiving of irregular sparsity — which is why §7.4's accelerators all add a separate predict/prune stage rather than making the array sparse.
PE (Processing Element)One cell of such an array. "Load imbalance across PEs" is the ASIC version of warp divergence.
DMA / descriptorDirect Memory Access: a copy engine that moves data without occupying compute units. A descriptor is the small record telling it what to move. §7.5's headline recommendation — a block-descriptor gather engine — is asking for a DMA whose unit is a KV block.
Arithmetic intensityFLOPs performed per byte moved. Compare it against the hardware's ridge point (peak FLOP/s ÷ peak bandwidth, ~295 on an H100) to tell whether you are compute- or memory-bound. §7.3 is entirely about raising this number.
Amdahl's lawIf a part of the work takes fraction fff of the runtime, speeding only that part up by sss gives overall speedup 1(1−f)+f/s\frac1{(1-f)+f/s}(1−f)+f/s1​. Making attention infinitely fast when attention is 20% of the time caps you at 1.25×. The reason §0.2 insists on knowing attention's share before optimising it.

B.2 Theory and notation

TermMeaning, and where it appears
Turing completeAble to simulate any computation, given unbounded time and memory. An expressiveness claim that says nothing about efficiency, and one that always rests on idealisations real hardware violates. §3 (BigBird), and the SUBLEQ instruction in the looped-transformer guide.
Universal approximatorCan approximate any function in some class to arbitrary accuracy, given enough capacity. Again an existence result: it does not say training will find the approximation, or that the required width is reasonable.
Expander graphA graph that is sparse (few edges per node) yet strongly connected, so any two nodes are joined by a short — O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) — path. Random sparse graphs are expanders with high probability, which is the theoretical justification for BigBird's random attention. §3.
Big-O and ΩO(f)O(f)O(f) is an upper bound up to constant factors ("no worse than"); Ω(f)\Omega (f)Ω(f) is a lower bound ("at least this much"). A result stated with Ω\Omega Ω is a hardness claim. Note that constants matter enormously in practice — see the FlashAttention crossover discussion in §4.
Pareto frontierThe set of configurations where you cannot improve one objective (say accuracy) without hurting another (say cost). "Improves the Pareto frontier" is the honest way to state a sparse-attention result: not "80% fewer FLOPs" but "better accuracy at equal measured cost." §5.2, §8.
Top-kkkSelecting the kkk largest elements of a list. Every content-aware sparse method ends in one. Cost depends on how many candidates: over n/Bn/Bn/B block scores it is cheap; over 128K individual tokens it is not — which is another argument for block granularity. §7.1, §7.4.
Softmaxsoftmax⁡(x)i=exi∑jexj\operatorname{softmax}(x)_i=\frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_je^{x_j}}softmax(x)i​=∑j​exj​exi​​ normalizes scores to sum to one. Changing the retained set changes the normalization. Initial attention sinks are a learned empirical behavior; normalization alone does not require a designated first-token sink.
L1 normalisationDividing a vector by the sum of its absolute values so the entries sum to 1 — i.e. turning scores into a distribution without a softmax. Used in DSA's indexer training (§6.3) to build a target distribution from raw attention scores.
KL divergence KL⁡(p∥q)\operatorname{KL}(p \| q)KL(p∥q)A non-symmetric measure of how far distribution qqq is from ppp; zero exactly when they match. DSA trains its cheap indexer by minimising the KL between the real attention distribution and the indexer's (§6.3) — the standard way to make a small model imitate a big one.
Perplexityexp⁡\expexp of the average negative log-likelihood per token — "how surprised the model is." Low perplexity means good next-token prediction, but it is dominated by easy, locally-predictable tokens, which is precisely why §8 warns it is nearly blind to long-range retrieval failures.
RULER / needle-in-a-haystackLong-context benchmarks. The needle test hides one verbatim fact in filler and asks for it back — easy. RULER adds multi-hop, aggregation and tracing tasks requiring many spread-out positions at once — much harder, and the right test for sparse attention.

CGlossary

A-shapeA head that attends to initial sink tokens plus a local band — the union of "sink" and "window."
Attention sinkA position that repeatedly receives substantial attention mass, often an initial token. Removing such positions can severely hurt checkpoints that rely on them; the effect depends on training, positional encoding, and cache policy.
Block-sparseSparsity whose unit is a contiguous tile of 64–128 tokens, so one decision skips one tensor-core tile.
Content-agnostic / content-awareWhether the pattern depends on the actual keys and queries. Fixed windows are agnostic; top-k selection is aware.
EvictionPermanently deleting KV entries. Reduces capacity; irreversible.
IndexerA small, low-precision network that scores KV entries so the expensive attention only runs on the survivors (DSA).
Online softmaxComputing softmax as a streaming reduction over tiles by carrying a running max and sum (§A.2).
Retrieval headA head that genuinely uses distant context, as opposed to a streaming head that only needs sinks + a local window.
RULERA long-context benchmark suite with multi-hop and aggregation tasks — much harder than single-needle retrieval.
SelectionSkipping the reading of KV entries while keeping them in the cache. Per-query, reversible.
Vertical-slashA head whose attention concentrates on a few fixed columns plus strided diagonals, with content-dependent positions.

DCheck yourself

1. A method reports 90% attention sparsity and 1.05× end-to-end decode speedup. What are the three most likely explanations?

(a) It still reads the KV it decides to skip — selection computed after the fetch saves arithmetic that was free anyway. (b) The sparsity is unstructured, so the kernel issues the same tensor-core tiles and just wastes lanes, plus pays gather overhead. (c) Attention wasn't the bottleneck at that context length — at short contexts the MLPs and weight loading dominate, and Amdahl's law does the rest. A fourth possibility: the index/scoring pass costs as much as it saves. §0.3, §7.1.

2. Why is block or page structure often useful for GPU sparse attention?

A dense tensor-core instruction consumes a fixed-shape tile, so zeroing arbitrary entries inside an already-issued tile does not save that instruction. However, selection can save work by gathering retained token rows into compact tiles, skipping pages, or using a purpose-built sparse kernel. Blocks often reduce metadata and make loads more coalesced; they are not a mathematical requirement for every speedup. DSA-style shared token selection illustrates why token granularity should not be ruled out. Account for executed tiles, fetched cache lines, index construction, and gather overhead. §4, §7.2.

3. Why can removing initial attention sinks severely damage a streaming model?

Some trained heads assign substantial attention mass to initial tokens even when those tokens carry little task content. Removing them changes the normalization and the weighted output; the retained-mass error derivation makes the local effect explicit. StreamingLLM reports a severe perplexity increase in its studied sink-removal setting. This is an empirical dependence of those checkpoints and cache policies, not a theorem that softmax requires an initial sink or that removing any first token always destroys every model. Evaluate the selected checkpoint, position scheme, and task. §2.1.

4. You share a GQA group's selected KV blocks across all 8 query heads in the group. What does that buy beyond code simplicity?

An 8× improvement in arithmetic intensity. Sparsity alone cuts FLOPs and bytes proportionally, so the FLOP/byte ratio — and hence your position on the roofline — is unchanged; you only go faster in proportion to bytes saved. Sharing the selection means one KV block load feeds 8 heads' worth of arithmetic: the numerator scales, the denominator doesn't. It also removes load imbalance within the group. This is NSA's central kernel decision. §7.3.

5. Distinguish selection from eviction and explain how recoverability changes the trade.

Selection chooses which stored KV entries a particular query reads. It usually reduces attention traffic while retaining capacity use at that storage level. Eviction removes entries from a particular cache and can free capacity; entries may remain recoverable from a lower memory tier, raw context plus recomputation, or a separate archive. Permanently discarding all representations and source text makes later retrieval impossible. Choose a policy using bandwidth, capacity, transfer/recomputation cost, and measured retrieval quality, rather than treating every eviction as equally irreversible. §1.1.

6. Why did the 2019–2021 fixed-pattern methods largely fail to reach production?

Three reasons compounding. Content-agnostic masks cannot retrieve the one relevant passage far back, and perplexity — the metric everyone reported — is nearly blind to that failure. They required pre-training from scratch with the pattern, while the frontier was training dense. And FlashAttention made the exact baseline ~7× faster in wall clock, so a 2× theoretical FLOP saving stopped being interesting. What survived is the vocabulary and the sliding-window layer itself. §3.

7. A₃ and SpAtten both prune attention. Why does only one of them help generative decoding?

Because of when the pruning decision is made relative to the DRAM fetch. A³ sorts key dimensions and approximates scores — but it must read all the keys from DRAM to do so, so DRAM traffic is unchanged and only compute falls. That helps compute-bound encoders and does nothing for memory-bound decode. SpAtten's cascade pruning decides from accumulated scores of previous layers, before fetching this layer's Q/K/V, so the traffic genuinely drops — 10× measured. Prune before you fetch. §7.4.

8. What single metric change would most improve the sparse-attention literature?

Plotting accuracy against measured cost (latency or bytes moved) instead of against nominal sparsity, separately for prefill and decode, with the index cost included, and reporting the worst task rather than the average. The Sparse Frontier's headline framing follows from doing this: the correct claim is "a larger sparse model beats a smaller dense one at equal cost," not "80% of the FLOPs removed." §8.

9. You are specifying an inference ASIC. Name the one hardware unit that most helps sparse attention, and one thing not to build.

Build: a block-descriptor DMA / gather engine whose unit is a KV block rather than a cache line — hand it a list of block IDs and let it issue coalesced bursts. Everything else (top-kkk, low-precision scoring path) is cheap by comparison, and without the gather engine the rest is wasted. Don't build: element-granularity sparsity support, or anything that assumes a static mask — modern patterns are content-dependent and change every token. §7.5.

10. Why do all three Era-3 methods (NSA, MoBA, DSA) separate a cheap scoring pass from the attention pass?

Because content-aware sparsity is only worth it if deciding costs much less than doing. Each solves it differently — NSA derives scores as a by-product of its compression branch (nearly free), MoBA scores against mean-pooled block centroids (O(n/B)O(n/B)O(n/B)), DSA uses a narrow FP8 MQA indexer (small constant factor). The pattern is identical to SpAtten's progressive quantization: fetch and compute at low precision to decide, then spend full precision only on what survives. §6, §7.4.
